newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Three-day truce raises hope of calm in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Three-day truce raises hope of calm in Brazzaville.

text.p: Brazzaville hoped for a pause in bloody clashes on Wednesday after warring factions carving up the Congolese capital agreed to a three-day ceasefire.

Neither the president's men nor rivals who back a former Marxist military leader said what would happen at the weekend when the truce -- at least the second to be called since fighting flared on June 5 -- is due to expire.

The United States decided not to wait to find out. Ambassador Aubrey Hooks said he and the other 11 Americans at the embassy would pull out on Wednesday to the city of Kinshasa across the Congo river in the former Zaire.
"We are leaving, very regretfully so, because of the security situation and the fact there is no assurance the airport will stay open once the French leave," he told Reuters by telephone.
France is withdrawing its 1,250 troops who helped evacuate more than 5,500 foreigners from the city in dangerous conditions. Around half the soldiers had flown out by Tuesday.
"We expect to stick to our plan and that by Saturday afternoon there will be no French military left here," army spokesman Col Henry Pelissier said from Brazzaville.
He said the city had been calmer on Tuesday, though with some mortar and gunfire, especially as the ceasefire that was announced by French ambassador Raymond Cesaire neared.
Fighting broke out on June 5 between armed forces backing President Pascal Lissouba and his once Marxist predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Sassou Nguesso ran the country from 1979 to 1992, when Lissouba defeated him in multi-party elections. They were rival candidates for presidential elections next month that both men say now look doomed.
Bodies lie rotting in streets of the capital that are too dangerous to enter. The international Red Cross said 200 bodies were picked up in the first 48 hours of the fighting alone.

The airport, which the French had been guarding, is in the firing line between the two forces which have carved up control of much of the city that until recently seemed like a haven of peace while war raged in neighbouring Zaire.
The two sides agreed to treat the airport as a neutral zone during the ceasefire to be used for humanitarian purposes.
Cesaire said both sides would meet again on Wednesday to discuss the situation.

A third militia controls southern parts of Brazzaville, beside the river frontier, but has so far stayed neutral under city mayor Bernard Kolelas, who helped broker the latest ceasefire at the French embassy.
Wider peace talks in the capital of neighbouring Gabon failed on Tuesday to make any progress. U.N. special representative Mohamed Sahnoun said he was deeply disappointed.
An African peacekeeping force is one suggestion under discussion.

France, the former colonial master, turned down a request by Lissouba that its troops should stay to form a buffer zone in the city or join a larger foreign force, but said it would keep its embassy open.
